title: India's Homegrown CAR-T Cell Therapies Are Reshaping Blood Cancer Treatment
excerpt: With two approved indigenous CAR-T therapies and over 600 patients treated, India has emerged as a global hub for affordable cell and gene therapy — at one-tenth the cost of Western alternatives.
body:
• India now has two regulator-approved indigenous CAR-T cell therapies — NexCAR19 (approved October 2023) and Qartemi (approved January 2025) — both targeting CD19-positive B-cell blood cancers at roughly one-tenth the cost of comparable U.S. treatments.
  • NexCAR19, developed by IIT Bombay spin-off ImmunoACT with Tata Memorial Centre, has been administered to more than 600 patients, with clinical trials showing a 70% overall response rate and results matching the best international data.
  • India's affordable CAR-T model is expanding internationally, with Cipla partnering to bring ImmunoACT's therapy to Africa, while a third Indian effort — Cellogen Therapeutics — is developing next-generation bispecific CAR-T cells for trials at CMC Vellore.

A Revolution Born in Mumbai Labs

In 2015, Alka Dwivedi, then a graduate student at the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, began exploring whether a CAR-T cell therapy — one of the most advanced forms of cancer immunotherapy — could be designed and manufactured in India. A decade later, that question has been answered definitively.

https://x.com/CMEINDIA1/status/2093009002716434470

India has become one of only a handful of countries in the world that develops, manufactures, and delivers chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy within its own borders. Two indigenous products, NexCAR19 and Qartemi, have received approval from India's Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation, giving patients with relapsed or refractory B-cell blood cancers — acute lymphoblastic leukemia and non-Hodgkin lymphoma — a treatment option that costs ₹30 to 50 lakh ($36,000 to $60,000), compared to $400,000 or more in the United States.

CAR-T cell therapy works by extracting a patient's own T cells, genetically engineering them in a laboratory to recognize and attack cancer cells carrying a specific marker (CD19 in these therapies), multiplying them, and infusing them back into the patient. It is a personalized treatment — each dose is manufactured from the individual patient's blood.

NexCAR19: From IIT Lab to 600 Patients

NexCAR19, known generically as actalycabtagene autoleucel, was developed by Prof. Rahul Purwar and his team at IIT Bombay's Department of Biosciences and Bioengineering in collaboration with Dr. Gaurav Narula and the oncology team at Tata Memorial Centre in Mumbai. ImmunoACT, a spin-off company founded by Purwar in 2018, manufactures and commercializes the therapy.

The development journey included training at the U.S. National Cancer Institute's Center for Cancer Research, where Dwivedi and colleagues worked alongside American CAR-T experts to refine their approach. The team designed a humanized CAR construct aimed at reducing side effects — a critical consideration for patients in India's largely self-pay healthcare system.

Phase I and II clinical trials enrolled 64 patients with advanced lymphoma or leukemia. According to data presented at the American Society of Hematology meeting, 67% of evaluable patients showed a significant decrease in cancer, with approximately half achieving complete response — results that matched the best international studies, according to India's Drug Controller General.

"This is like a dream come true and an incredible win for the patients in India. Now our patients in India and countries with limited resources will have access to this lifesaving drug at an affordable cost."

— Rahul Purwar, Founder and CEO, ImmunoACT

A Second Therapy and a Growing Pipeline

India's CAR-T ecosystem expanded further in January 2025 when Qartemi (varnimcabtagene autoleucel), developed by Bengaluru-based Immuneel Therapeutics, received approval for adult relapsed or refractory B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma. The IMAGINE trial reported an approximately 83% response rate at 90 days. Qartemi is priced at ₹35 to 50 lakh.

A third effort is underway. Delhi-based startup Cellogen Therapeutics has received patent approval for the world's first indigenously developed bispecific third-generation CAR-T cells. Backed by $2 million in funding from NATCO Pharma, clinical trials are planned in collaboration with Christian Medical College, Vellore.

The international dimension is growing as well. Cipla has partnered with ImmunoACT to bring talicabtagene autoleucel (the renamed commercial version of NexCAR19) to Africa, where blood cancers affect thousands of patients annually with virtually no access to CAR-T therapy.

Why Cost Matters

In the United States, FDA-approved CAR-T therapies such as Kymriah and Yescarta carry list prices exceeding $400,000, with total treatment costs often surpassing $500,000 when hospitalization and supportive care are included. India's indigenous therapies cost roughly one-tenth of that — a differential driven by lower staffing, facility construction, and manufacturing costs.

This price gap has profound implications. India reports over 120,000 new blood cancer cases and 70,000 deaths annually, according to GLOBOCAN data. Asia accounts for the highest global prevalence of leukemia (45.8%), non-Hodgkin lymphoma (40.9%), and multiple myeloma (37.1%), yet until recently had almost no locally manufactured CAR-T options.

What's Next

ImmunoACT is scaling manufacturing capacity with a larger facility in Navi Mumbai and has partnered with more than 30 oncology hospitals across India. The company aims to treat approximately 1,200 patients per year. For the broader Indian healthcare sector, the CAR-T story represents a proof of concept: that advanced cell and gene therapies can be developed, manufactured, and delivered domestically in a middle-income country, potentially becoming a model for other nations seeking affordable access to cutting-edge cancer treatment.
